mainEntity.name: Is it safe to wait a few weeks before having a root canal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Whether a short delay is safe depends entirely on the condition of the tooth. In some cases, a brief wait may not significantly change the prognosis, particularly if the infection is in its early stages and there are no acute symptoms. However, in other cases — especially where there is active infection, swelling, or significant pain — delaying even a few weeks could allow the condition to worsen. Your dentist can advise on how urgently treatment is needed based on a clinical assessment. If you are experiencing worsening symptoms while waiting, it is important to contact your dental practice promptly.

mainEntity.name: Can antibiotics replace the need for a root canal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Antibiotics may be prescribed by your dentist to help manage an active infection, particularly if there is swelling or if the infection is spreading. However, antibiotics alone do not resolve the underlying problem — the infected or damaged tissue inside the tooth remains. Antibiotics can reduce symptoms temporarily, but without removing the source of infection through root canal treatment or extraction, the problem is likely to return. Antibiotics are best viewed as a supportive measure rather than a definitive treatment for an infected tooth pulp.

mainEntity.name: Will I definitely lose my tooth if I delay treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Some teeth can still be successfully treated after a period of delay, depending on the extent of damage and infection. However, the longer treatment is postponed, the greater the risk that complications may arise that could make the tooth unrestorable. Each case is unique, and the only reliable way to determine the current status of your tooth and the available treatment options is through a clinical examination with your dentist.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my toothache means I need a root canal?

acceptedAnswer.text: A toothache can have many causes, and not all toothaches indicate the need for a root canal. However, certain characteristics may suggest pulp involvement, such as spontaneous pain, lingering sensitivity to hot or cold, pain that wakes you at night, or swelling near the affected tooth. A thorough clinical examination, often including X-rays, is required to determine the cause of your symptoms and whether root canal treatment is appropriate. Self-diagnosis is not recommended, as other conditions can mimic similar symptoms.

Modern root canal treatment is carried out under local anaesthetic, which numbs the area and ensures you should not feel pain during the procedure. Many patients report that the experience is similar to having a filling placed. Some mild discomfort or tenderness may be felt for a few days after treatment, but this is usually manageable with over-the-counter pain relief. If you have concerns about dental anxiety or discomfort, discussing your worries with your dentist beforehand can help ensure you feel supported throughout the process.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I choose extraction instead of a root canal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Tooth extraction is an alternative to root canal treatment and may be recommended in certain situations, particularly if the tooth is severely damaged or unrestorable. However, losing a tooth can have consequences for your oral health, including shifting of adjacent teeth, changes to your bite, and bone loss in the area where the tooth was removed. If a tooth is extracted, your dentist will usually discuss replacement options with you. Where possible, preserving your natural tooth through root canal treatment is generally considered the preferred approach.
